sec.t:
One of the earliest stars was Sukumar Ray. His Bengali book of [[@sukumar-ray|nonsense verse]], *Abol Tabol*, came out in 1923 and is still recited by children in Kolkata. His son, the film-maker Satyajit Ray, later wrote the Feluda detective stories and edited *Sandesh*, the children's magazine his grandfather Upendrakishore Ray Chowdhury had started in 1913. Three generations of one family kept Bengali children reading for most of a century.

Ruskin Bond, born in 1934, has written for more than seventy years. His stories about the hills around Mussoorie and Dehradun, such as *The Blue Umbrella*, read like letters from a friend. He still lives in Landour, near Mussoorie, and children write to him from all over India. In Gujarat, a teacher named Gijubhai Badheka wrote simple stories for small children in the 1920s and changed how many schools thought about early learning.

From the 1990s, new publishers changed what Indian picture books looked like. Tulika Books in Chennai and Tara Books, also in Chennai, worked with folk artists and printed stories in several languages at once. Pratham Books, started in 2004, set out to put "a book in every child's hand" at a low price.

Writers today cover everything from cricket to climate. Paro Anand writes about hard subjects for teenagers. Ranjit Lal writes about birds and animals, often with plenty of jokes. Subhadra Sen Gupta, who died in 2021, made Indian history lively for young readers. And Sudha Murty's grandmother tales sell in huge numbers in both English and Kannada.

India has 22 languages listed in its Constitution and hundreds of others, which makes [[@translation|translation]] a big part of children's publishing. A good story written in Marathi may reach far more children once it is translated into Hindi or English.

Pratham Books' free website, StoryWeaver, launched in 2015. Anyone can read, print or translate its picture books, and volunteers have produced versions in hundreds of [[@languages-india|languages]]. A child in a village where nobody has ever printed a book in her mother tongue can now read one on a school tablet.

The Sahitya Akademi, India's national academy of letters, gives the Bal Sahitya Puraskar to children's writers in 24 languages each year. Book fairs in Kolkata, Delhi and other cities draw huge crowds of families. The Kolkata fair, held every winter, is one of the busiest book fairs anywhere, and many children buy their first book of their own there. Smaller fairs and school libraries matter just as much. A writer can only reach a child if the book is actually on a shelf nearby.

text: A pancake is one of the easiest foods a person can make. Mix [[@grains-world|ground grain]] with water or milk, pour it onto something hot, and in a minute you have food. You do not need an oven, yeast or a lot of skill.

Since almost every culture grows some kind of grain and has fire, almost every culture invented pancakes. What changes is the grain and the treatment. India uses rice, [[@lentils-world|lentils]] and gram flour to make [[@dosa-idli|dosa]], uttapam and cheela. Ethiopia uses teff. France uses wheat for thin crêpes, and Americans add baking powder to make thick, fluffy stacks. China has jianbing, Russia has blini, and [[@seoul|Korea]] has pajeon, a pancake full of spring onions.

st.prompt: Why does the first pancake or dosa from a pan often come out badly?

options.t: The pan is not yet evenly hot and oiled
The batter at the top of the bowl is weaker
The first one always sticks for no reason

st.reveal: A pan takes time to heat evenly, and the first pancake soaks up extra oil and spreads the heat. By the second one, the pan is hot all over and the surface is seasoned, so the batter browns evenly.

d.try: Put a spoon of baking soda in a glass and add a spoon of lemon juice. Watch the fizz. Those bubbles are carbon dioxide, the same gas that baking soda or baking powder makes inside pancake batter to puff it up.
myth: The first pancake fails because of bad luck.
It is physics, not luck. The pan's surface is still heating unevenly and the oil has not spread properly. Cooks in many countries throw away, or quietly eat, the first one for this reason.
facts: flour or ground grain, liquid, a hot surface

sec.t:
A heavy, flat pancake is fine, but people like them light. There are two main ways to get bubbles into batter.

The old way is [[@fermentation|fermentation]]. Dosa batter, made of soaked rice and urad dal ground together, is left overnight. Wild [[yeast|yeast]] and bacteria feed on it and give off gas, so the batter rises and turns slightly sour. Ethiopian injera and Indian appam use the same trick.

The newer way is chemistry. Baking soda, and baking powder, which became common in the 1800s, react with acid and moisture to release carbon dioxide in minutes. That is how American pancakes rise on the griddle, with tiny holes popping on top just before you flip.

In Ethiopia and Eritrea, a meal is often served on one enormous, soft, spongy pancake called injera. It is made from teff, a tiny grain grown in the Ethiopian highlands for thousands of years. The batter ferments for days, and the finished injera is full of holes and slightly sour.

Stews and vegetables are spooned on top. Diners tear off pieces of injera with their right hand and use them to scoop up food, a bit like eating with roti. When the stews are finished, the plate is eaten too.

In Britain, Shrove Tuesday is called Pancake Day. It falls just before Lent, a time when many Christians traditionally gave up rich foods. Pancakes used up the eggs, milk and butter in the house. In the town of Olney, women run a race each year flipping a pancake in a frying pan, a custom said to date back to the 1400s.

In Russia, people eat piles of blini during Maslenitsa, [[@festival-foods|a festival marking the end of winter]]. The round, golden blini are often said to look like the returning sun.

When batter hits a hot pan, sugars and proteins in it react to make hundreds of new flavour and colour chemicals. Food scientists call this part of [[@cooking-science|cooking science]] the Maillard reaction, and it is why a crisp dosa and a golden pancake smell so good. The same reaction browns toast, roasted peanuts and the crust of bread.

text: Indian pickles, called achar, are fruits or vegetables preserved with salt, oil, spices and often something sour, like lemon juice or vinegar. [[@mango-varieties|Raw mango]], lemon, [[@citrus|lime]], chilli, carrot and gooseberry (amla) are common. They are cut into pieces, mixed with salt and spices like [[@mustard|mustard]], fenugreek, turmeric and chilli, and packed into jars with oil.

The salt draws water out, the oil seals out air, and the sourness makes life hard for germs. Many pickles also sit in the sun for days to help them mature. A good pickle can keep for a year or more, adding a burst of flavour to a simple meal of dal and rice.

st.prompt: Why do families use a completely dry spoon to take pickle out of the jar?

options.t: Water can let mould and microbes grow and spoil the pickle
A wet spoon makes the oil taste bitter
Water makes the spices lose their colour

st.reveal: Pickles keep because salt, oil and acid leave very little free water for microbes to live in. A splash of water from a wet spoon gives mould a foothold. That's why careful families keep pickle spoons dry.

myth: Pickles keep forever and can never go bad.

Well-made pickles last a long time, often a year or more, but they can still spoil. Too little salt or oil, or water getting into the jar, can let mould grow. A pickle that smells odd or has fuzzy spots should be thrown away.

sec.t:
Food spoils when bacteria, yeasts and moulds grow in it. These microbes need water. Salt pulls water out of the fruit and out of microbes too, by a process called osmosis. With little free water left, most harmful microbes can't survive.

Oil covers the pickle and keeps out air, which moulds need. Sour ingredients like lemon juice, vinegar or the natural acid in raw mango make the pickle too acidic for many germs. Spices such as turmeric and mustard add flavour and may help slow the growth of some microbes too. Together, these tricks let families [[@food-preserve|preserve food]] long before anyone had a fridge.

In many Indian homes, pickle-making is a summer event. When raw mangoes appear in markets, families buy them by the kilo. The [[@mango-tree|mangoes]] are washed, dried completely and chopped, often with a special cutter for the hard stone.

In Andhra Pradesh, the famous avakaya is made with raw mango pieces, mustard powder, red chilli powder, salt and sesame oil. In Punjab, mango pickle uses mustard oil and fennel. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, tiny whole raw mangoes are pickled in brine to make vadu manga.

The jars are often set out in the sun for several days, stirred each day. The heat helps the salt and spices soak in.

In the USA, "pickle" usually means a cucumber pickle. Many are kept in vinegar, while traditional dill pickles are fermented in salty water. Both use the same basic ideas as Indian achar: salt and acid stop spoiling microbes.

The big difference is oil and spice. American pickles are mostly sour and salty. Indian pickles are often hot, oily and strongly spiced, and a small spoonful goes a long way.

Families have rules for pickle jars, and most of them make scientific sense. Use a clean, dry spoon. Keep the lid tight. Make sure there's always a layer of oil on top. Store the jar in a cool, dry place.

If water gets in, mould can grow. That's why pickles are made in the dry summer heat, why fruit is dried well before pickling, and why a grandmother will not let anyone dip a wet spoon in her jar.
